title: Accel reportedly in talks to lead $1B round for Thinking Machines at $40B valuation
content:
Thinking Machines, the AI lab founded early last year by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati, is in discussions to raise $1 billion at a valuation of at least $40 billion, The Information reported Thursday. Existing backer Accel is in talks to lead the fundraise, according to our source and The Information’s reporting.
The new round, if it is completed, would value the company below the $50 billion valuation that Thinking Machines reportedly sought to secure late last year.
Thinking Machines’ annual revenue run rate stands at over $100 million, according to a source with knowledge of the company’s financials. At that revenue figure, a $40 billion valuation reflects an extraordinarily high revenue multiple.
Accel and Thinking Machines didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
In July, the company introduced Inkling, an open-weight model that generates revenue by charging usage-based compute fees for adapting models on proprietary data on its Tinker platform.
The startup’s prior fundraise — a $2 billion round that stands among the largest seed financings in history — valued the company at $12 billion. Andreessen Horowitz led the investment, joined by Nvidia, GV, Lightspeed, and Conviction Partners. Investors backed the round largely on the pedigree of Murati and the former OpenAI researchers who joined her.
Thinking Machines has since had several high-profile departures, with some of the co-founders, including Lilian Weng and Luke Metz, going back to OpenAI.

report.summary: Accel is in talks to lead a $1B funding round for Thinking Machines at a $40B valuation, sources say.
report.background: Thinking Machines, the AI lab founded by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati in 2025, has quickly become one of the most richly valued startups in artificial intelligence. The company reportedly generated over $100 million in annual recurring revenue, yet a $40 billion valuation would imply a staggering revenue multiple, highlighting how investor enthusiasm for top-tier AI talent and frontier research remains intense. This new round would mark a dramatic increase from the startup’s previous $12 billion valuation from a record-setting $2 billion seed financing led by Andreessen Horowitz with participation from Nvidia, GV, Lightspeed, and Conviction Partners. However, it would be below the $50 billion valuation the company reportedly sought late last year, suggesting that concerns about high-profile co-founder departures may have tempered expectations. The funding landscape for AI labs remains volatile, with investors balancing massive capital needs against questions about long-term differentiation and revenue sustainability.
key_points: Accel, an existing investor, is reportedly in talks to lead a $1 billion investment into Thinking Machines at a valuation of at least $40 billion, according to The Information and TechCrunch sources. The round has not been finalized, and neither Accel nor Thinking Machines commented publicly.

The new valuation is lower than the $50 billion Thinking Machines reportedly sought late last year, implying that market conditions or internal turbulence may have forced the company to adjust its expectations downward. Still, a $40 billion valuation would be a massive step up from the $12 billion figure set during its record-breaking $2 billion seed round.

Despite the enormous valuation, the company’s annual revenue run rate is only about $100 million, according to a person familiar with its finances. That means the valuation is roughly 400 times revenue, an exceptionally high multiple that places immense pressure on the lab to rapidly scale monetization and prove its models can sustain commercial demand.

Thinking Machines launched Inkling in July, an open-weight model designed to generate revenue by charging usage-based compute fees when customers adapt models on proprietary data using its Tinker platform. This business model reflects a broader industry shift away from simply selling access to frontier models and toward controlled fine-tuning and enterprise-specific deployment services.

The startup has faced notable attrition, with several co-founders including Lilian Weng and Luke Metz departing to rejoin OpenAI. These exits raise questions about talent retention and technical leadership stability, though Murati’s reputation and the remaining research team continue to anchor investor confidence.

The potential deal underscores how much capital is still flowing into elite AI labs, despite broader skepticism about lofty valuations and unproven revenue models. Success will depend on whether Thinking Machines can convert research breakthroughs into durable, high-margin enterprise revenue while retaining top AI talent amid fierce competition from established players.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reported round signals that leading venture firms still see enormous strategic value in funding top-tier AI research labs, even when current revenue is tiny relative to valuation. It also suggests that the competitive battleground is shifting from raw model capability to enterprise adaptation platforms and specialized inference services, as seen with Inkling and Tinker. Developers should watch how Thinking Machines prices and packages its open-weight models, since that could influence broader norms for model licensing, fine-tuning, and compute-based monetization. For regular users, sustained funding means more competition in AI assistants and tooling, potentially leading to better features and lower prices. However, the valuation gap also carries risk: if revenue growth stalls, future down rounds or consolidation may follow.
report.tools: To follow Thinking Machines’ technology, watch for the open-weight Inkling model on Hugging Face, where weights and model cards are typically shared. The Tinker platform is the commercial entry point for adapting models on proprietary data; a free tier or developer preview may be offered. Also monitor Accel’s portfolio announcements and OpenAI’s open-source releases for market context. Researchers interested in fine-tuning techniques can track the project’s documentation and GitHub repository for benchmark scripts and example workflows.
